finding.claim: Delete authorization check is a no-op: the boolean returned by is_allowed (aliased require_allowed) is discarded, so any caller can delete any stored file.
finding.source: DELETE /files/<fid> path parameter; no authentication required

trace.note: is_allowed imported under the name require_allowed
require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") called with return value discarded
is_allowed returns a bool and never raises or aborts

finding.guards_checked: load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and enforces nothing; acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) would abort correctly but this route does not call it. Severity HIGH, not CRITICAL: attacker must know a valid fid (Check 13 Q1). Validation Tier 0.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only guard is is_allowed (imported as require_allowed at views.py:4), which returns a bool (acl.py:4-5). Its result is discarded by the bare call at views.py:18, so nothing aborts before the delete at views.py:19. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, which calls abort(403)) is imported at views.py:3 but never called on the delete route. load_user (views.py:10-12) only reads a header and enforces nothing.
verdict.reason: The bool returned by is_allowed is discarded at views.py:18, so the unconditional `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including an anonymous one with no X-Session-User-Verified header; the abort-on-deny helper ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is never called on this route.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the unverified client header X-Session-User-Verified, allowing impersonation of any named user with grants if the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that overwrites the header.
finding.sink: g.user used as authorization principal at views.py:18, views.py:26, and acl.py:5

trace.note: header copied into g.user in before_request with no validation
grants.get(user, []) keyed on the spoofable name

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session, or token verification in repo. No proxy config in repo to confirm the header is stripped or overwritten. acl.py:5 returns [] for unknown users so the header is not a bypass by itself. Candidate only: depends on deployment. Validation Tier 0.

verdict.guard_found: acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed aborts with 403 when is_allowed is False and is used at views.py:26 (rename_file), which is effective for rename but does not stop spoofing a granted name. views.py:18 calls require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4), which returns a bool, but the result is a bare statement that is discarded, so it is not a guard at all for delete_file. No signature, session, or proxy-stripping control exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches (views.py:12 copies the header into g.user, views.py:26 and acl.py:5 use it as the principal), but whether an outside attacker can send X-Session-User-Verified depends on a proxy or ingress that is not in this repo (views.py:12 has no validation), so reachability cannot be decided here. Separately, views.py:18 discards the boolean from require_allowed, so DELETE /files/<fid> is unauthorized for any caller regardless of the header, a stronger issue than the one claimed.

finding.claim: Existence oracle: a missing fid raises KeyError (500) before the authorization check, while an existing but denied file returns 403, letting callers enumerate valid file IDs.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25, before any authorization check

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for missing IDs, returns 500
abort(403) for existing but denied files, distinguishing existence

finding.guards_checked: Severity LOW hardening only: no demonstrated primary vulnerability from this alone; IDs must still be known or guessed.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:17 and views.py:25 index STORE[fid] with no guard, so a missing ID raises KeyError (500). On the rename path, acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed aborts 403, but only after the lookup at views.py:25. On the delete path, views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is is_allowed (acl.py:4, 5), a bool-returning function whose result is discarded, so it enforces nothing. The g.user value comes from a client-settable header (views.py:12), which is a separate weakness.
verdict.reason: The existence oracle is real: a missing fid gives a 500 from the bare STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25, while an existing file on the rename path gets abort(403) at acl.py:10. The candidate's trace is accurate for rename but omits the delete path, where views.py:18 discards is_allowed's bool, so an existing file is deleted with 200 instead of 403, which is a stronger authorization bypass than the candidate reports.
